About the Simulation

Visualizing the high-energy harmonic oscillator in natural units ℏ = m = ω = 1.

As n → ∞, ΔE/Eₙ → 0: the spacing between nearby energy levels becomes small compared with the total energy.

Key physics: The probability density |ψ_n(x)|² is time-independent for an energy eigenstate. The wavefunction panel shows the phase rotation through Re(ψ) and Im(ψ), while the probability panel compares |ψ_n(x)|² with the classical distribution.

The orange classical curve diverges at the turning points, so the display clips only the visible height near those endpoints. The shaded region is there to make the classical support easier to compare with the quantum probability density.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A ladder sixty rungs high

We’re going to climb high today. This is the harmonic oscillator taken far up its energy ladder: n runs from 0 to 60. The top panel holds the potential V(x) = ½x², with the energy Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω of the chosen state drawn across it in gold; below it you’ll find the eigenfunction ψₙ(x,t), blue for its real part and pink for its imaginary part. We’re in natural units: ħ = m = ω = 1.

2 · Where the mass lingers

Let’s begin with no quantum mechanics at all. A classical mass on a spring swings back and forth between the two ends of its range. Compare a narrow strip at the centre with an equally narrow strip at one end. What do you think? Over many periods, the mass spends more time in…

3 · The lowest rung

Now drop all the way down to the ground state, n = 0. The orange classical curve is largest at the two ends of the swing. Where do you think the quantum |ψ₀(x)|² will be largest?

4 · Sixty rungs up

Now let’s make the same comparison right at the top of the ladder, n = 60. What’s your guess? Against the orange classical curve, the green |ψₙ(x)|² will be…

5 · Why nobody sees the rungs

One last question, and it’s a big one. Neighbouring rungs are ħω apart at every n, and the pendulum in a clock sits at around n = 10³⁰. So why do you think its energy looks continuous?

The Physics

The quantum harmonic oscillator · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim takes the quantum harmonic oscillator far up its energy ladder, to n = 60, and sets its probability density beside what a classical mass on a spring would do. It shows how the quantum picture and the classical one meet when the energy is large.

What you'll learn

  • Where the energy ladder Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω comes from, and what sets its rungs.
  • How a classical mass's position distribution follows from its speed.
  • How the quantum density |ψₙ(x)|² compares with that distribution from n = 0 to n = 60.
  • How one rung compares with the total energy as n changes, and what the time dependence of an eigenstate looks like.
The parabola V(x) = ½x² with the allowed energies drawn across it; one rung (gold) ends at its two turning points.

What's on screen

  • Top panel: the potential V(x) with every rung Eₙ; the state you picked is the gold one, with dashed turning points.
  • Blue: the real part of ψₙ(x,t), in the middle panel.
  • Pink: the imaginary part of ψₙ(x,t), in the middle panel.
  • Bottom panel: the probability density |ψₙ(x)|² in green.
  • Orange dashed curve: the classical distribution Pclassical(x), for a mass with the same energy.
  • Sidebar readouts: Classical Limit, Quantum Numbers, Turning Points and Time Evolution.
See itGo to the opening state, n = 40. Watch for: the gold rung and its dashed turning points on the top panel, and the three plots filled in below it.

03

The energy ladder

The well is the parabola V(x) = ½mω²x², which in the sim's units is V = ½x². Schrödinger's equation inside it is:

The potential on screen, and the equation each ψₙ must satisfy.

Only certain energies give a ψₙ that fits in the well and dies away outside it. They form a ladder:

The allowed energies, and the state belonging to each one.
  • Neighbouring rungs are ħω apart, whatever n is.
  • The lowest rung, E₀ = ½ħω, is the zero-point energy: the oscillator cannot be at rest at the bottom of the well.
  • Rung n meets the parabola at the turning points x = ±√(2n + 1), the dashed lines in the sim.
See itClimb the first rungs, n = 0 to 4, one at a time. Watch for: the gold rung rising by the same step each time, and the Energy readout going 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5.
04

Where a classical mass spends its time

A mass on a spring moves fastest through the centre and stops at each end of its swing. The time it spends in a thin strip dx is dx/|v|, so the strip's share of one period Tcl = 2π/ω is:

The classical distribution for a mass of energy Eₙ.
  • Pclassical(x) is lowest at the centre and rises toward the turning points, where the mass is slowest.
  • It diverges at ±xtp yet its total is still 1, so the sim clips the drawing there.
  • It contains no ħ. It is Newton's answer, drawn on the quantum plot for comparison.
See itGo to n = 60, where the turning points are at ±11.00. Watch for: the orange dashed curve lowest at the centre, rising toward both ends.
05

From the ground state to sixty rungs up

The green curve is a probability density: the probability of finding the particle in a strip dx is |ψₙ(x)|² dx, and the total over all x is 1.

  • n = 0: one Gaussian hump, tallest at the centre, where Pclassical is lowest. About 16% of the probability lies beyond the turning points at ±1.
  • n = 60: ψₙ has n nodes, so |ψₙ|² is 61 ripples between the turning points at ±11.00. Averaged over a few ripples it follows the orange curve; the tops reach about twice that height.
  • The ripples never go away. At n = 60 they are about 0.36 x₀ apart, and a detector that averages over a few of them sees only the orange curve.
Away from the turning points, |ψₙ|² is a fast cos² riding on the classical curve.
See itStep from n = 0 to n = 12 to n = 60. Watch for: one hump at n = 0, then ripples that crowd along the orange curve as n rises.
06

How big one rung is next to the energy

The gap Eₙ₊₁ − Eₙ = ħω is the same at every n. What changes is the gap measured against the energy of the state:

The absolute gap stays fixed; the relative gap is 1/(n + ½).
n

This slider moves the sim too.

  • ΔE/Eₙ is 2 at n = 0, 0.0247 at n = 40 and 0.0165 at n = 60.
  • The rungs do not merge: they stay ħω apart. Only their size next to Eₙ shrinks, until no measurement of the energy can resolve one rung.
See itStep n through 0, 5, 20 and 60. Watch for: the Classical Limit readout falling from 2 to 0.0165 while the gap stays 1.000.
07

What is moving on screen

An energy eigenstate is a fixed shape ψₙ(x) times a rotating phase:

The only time dependence is the phase factor.
  • Blue and pink are Re Ψₙ and Im Ψₙ. They share one shape and trade places as the phase turns.
  • Green is |Ψₙ|² = |ψₙ|². The phase cancels, so the density does not change in time. That is what stationary state means.
  • One turn of the phase takes Tphase = 2π/Eₙ: 1.80 at n = 3, 0.155 at n = 40. The classical period Tcl = 2π/ω = 6.283 is a separate number and does not depend on n.
See itPlay n = 3 at half speed. Watch for: the blue and pink curves trading places while the green curve does not move.
08

Where it matters

Two oscillators at opposite ends of the ladder.
  • Molecular vibrations. A CO molecule's stretch has ħω ≈ 0.27 eV, about ten times kBT at 300 K, so at room temperature it sits in n = 0 and its rungs show up in infrared spectra.
  • Everyday oscillators. A 1 kg pendulum with a 2 s period and a 1 cm amplitude sits near n ≈ 10³⁰. One rung is about 10⁻³⁰ of its energy, far below anything we can measure.
  • Near any minimum. The bottom of a smooth well is close to a parabola, so this oscillator is the first model for molecular bonds and for lattice vibrations in a crystal.
Go deeper: where the classical period comes back
  • A single eigenstate shows no motion in |Ψ|². Mix two neighbouring rungs and |Ψ|² oscillates at (Eₙ₊₁ − Eₙ)/ħ = ω, with period 2π/ω = Tcl.
  • The sim shows one eigenstate at a time, so this beat is not drawn.
09

Summary

In one line. The oscillator's rungs are always ħω apart, but their size next to Eₙ shrinks as 1/(n + ½), and by n = 60 the local average of the quantum density follows the classical curve.

Key points

  • Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω, with turning points at ±√(2n + 1).
  • Pclassical(x) is the time a classical mass spends in each strip, so it is largest where the mass is slowest.
  • |ψₙ|² has n nodes. At large n its local average follows Pclassical.
  • An eigenstate's phase turns at Eₙ/ħ, but |ψₙ|² never changes.

Common mix-ups

  • "The probability density sloshes back and forth like the classical mass." For an eigenstate, |ψₙ(x)|² has no t in it. Only the blue and pink curves change.
  • "At high n the rungs merge into a continuum." They stay exactly ħω apart. Only ΔE/Eₙ = 1/(n + ½) shrinks.
  • "En = nħω." The ½ is the zero-point energy. Without it E₀ would be 0.

Things to try on your own

  • Set n = 0, then n = 60. At each, note where the green curve is tallest and where the orange one is lowest.
  • Raise n from 0 to 12 and compare the Nodes readout with the number of dips in the green curve.
  • Read Tphase at n = 10 and n = 60 and check each against 2π/Eₙ.
